title: Shortest paths in a graph without lengths
description:
In an undirected graph whose edges have no lengths, the distance from one vertex to another is the fewest edges on any path between them. A shortest path to every vertex can be recorded by remembering, for each vertex, its parent: the vertex just before it on one shortest path from the source. Following parents back from any vertex until the source is reached walks one of its shortest paths in reverse.

Implement a function called UnweightedShortestPaths that receives the number of vertices, an adjacency list, and a source vertex, and returns two lists. The first holds, for each vertex, its distance from the source. The second holds, for each vertex, its parent. Vertices are numbered from zero, and the adjacency list gives, for each vertex, its neighbours; every edge appears in the lists of both of its ends.

With the edges 0-1, 1-2, 0-3, 3-4, 4-7, 3-7, 6-7, 4-5, 4-6, 5-6 and source 0:
UnweightedShortestPaths(8, adjacency, 0) -> distances [0, 1, 2, 1, 2, 3, 3, 2], parents [-1, 0, 1, 0, 3, 4, 4, 3]. Following parents back from 7 gives 7, 3, 0, so the shortest path from 0 to 7 is 0 3 7.

When several shortest paths exist, any one of them may be recorded: in the example above, vertex 6 could have parent 4 or parent 7, since both are two edges from the source. The hidden tests accept any parent that is a neighbour of the vertex and exactly one edge closer to the source. With the same edges and source 2, the distances are [2, 1, 0, 3, 4, 5, 5, 4], and one shortest path from 2 to 6 is 2 1 0 3 4 6.

The source has no parent, and neither does a vertex the source cannot reach; both get -1 as their parent, and an unreachable vertex also gets -1 as its distance. With the edges 0-1, 1-2, 3-4 and source 0:
UnweightedShortestPaths(5, adjacency, 0) -> distances [0, 1, 2, -1, -1], parents [-1, 0, 1, -1, -1].

The hidden tests also check a source that is not vertex 0, parallel edges between the same two vertices, an edge from a vertex to itself, and a single vertex.

This card asks for the optimal solution, and the tests enforce it: one of them is a graph of two hundred thousand vertices with a two second budget. Answers that lower the same distance again and again as shorter paths turn up give the right result but are far too slow to pass. Every vertex and every edge has to be handled a constant number of times, so the total work stays proportional to the number of vertices plus the number of edges.
objective: Recall breadth-first search as the linear-time way to find fewest-edge distances and a shortest-path parent for every vertex of an unweighted graph.

metadata.source: Shortest path in an unweighted graph, GeeksforGeeks (https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/shortest-path-unweighted-graph/)
